Epitope specific T cell lines were established by incubating donor's CD8+ cells with T2 cells in the presence of BMLF1 peptide for a minimum of 3 weeks.
Assay - Comments: Epitopic peptide-stimulated T cell lines from healthy, influenza and EBV-immune, individuals were tested for cross-reactivity agaisnt  Flu M1 peptide. Out of 7 donors cell lines that responded to BMLF1, 3 of those also responded to M1. Between 0.4 and 5.5% of the BMLF1-stimulated  cells are shown to recognize M1. A similar result is seen in the converse scenario, where M1 stimulated cell lines recognize BMLF1 peptide. The avidity of one cell line towards both peptides was determined by sensitization EC50 with titrated amounts of peptide, and is actually shown to be  higher for M1 (10^-9 M) than for BMLF1 (5x10^-7 M). When a T cell line was derived from one of this donors by in vitro costimulation with both M1 and EBV-BMLF1 peptides, a 0.4% of cells costained with both peptide-tetramer complexes, indicating  cross-recognition. Immunization - Comments: Epitope specific clones were obtained through sorting of CD8+ T cells followed by cloning. Clones were maintained by stimulation with EBV transformed LCL.

1st in vivo Process - Process Type: Environmental exposure to endemic/ubiquitous agent without evidence for disease
Immunization - Comments: Fifteen healthy laboratory donors were used for this study.  EBV-specific CTLs were generated by stimulating PBMCs with autologous, irradiated EBV (B95.8)-transformed LCLs. The generation of clones was described in Moss et al. Nature 1988;331:719.
Assay - Comments: Epitope-specific CTLs reacted with EBV (B95.8), as well as 4 other EBV isolates.

Immunization - Comments: HLA-A2+ or HLA-B8+ EBV+ age- and sex-matched healthy volunteers (n = 9) and quiescent immunosuppressed, solid organ transplant (IS SOTx) patients (multivisceral n=5 and small bowel n=4) were recruited. All patients were on daily prednisone and tacrolimus formore than 4 years, and were quiescent at the time of blood donation, without evidence of rejection or signs of EBV disease. DCs were pulsed with a pool of EBV peptides: BMLF1 (GLCTLVAML), BZLF1 (RAKFKQLL), LMP2 (CLGGLLTMV), EBNA3A (SVRDRLARL), and EBNA3A (FLRGRAYGL).

These effectors demonstrated a IFNg high and IL-5 low response suggesting a type I bias. Further, these epitope-specific CD8+ Tregs were found to actively suppress antigen non-cognate CD4+ T cell proliferation in a Ag-specific manner.

1st in vivo Process - Process Type: Environmental exposure to endemic/ubiquitous agent without evidence for disease
Immunization - Comments: PBMC were stimulated in vitro with the epitope and expanded in the presence of IL-2 and IL-5. Single CD8+, IFN-γ+ cells were cloned and expanded and tested for recognition of the epitope.
Assay - Comments: Epitope-specific CTL clones lysed human HLA-B8 islet cells in the presence of the epitope in  a dose-dependent manner. The amount of lysis varied between islet cells from different donors and was lower than observed with epitope-pulsed HLA-B8-transfected B cell line C1R.B8, but was significantly higher than with human islet cells not expressing HLA-B8. Epitope-specific CTL lysis of the islet cells was inhibited by concanamycin A, which causes perforin degradation, but was not affected by anti-FasL antibody or the pan-caspase inhibitor zVAD. The authors conclude that perforin plays a role in CTL lysis of islet cells, but not the Fas/FasL pathway. Preincubation of islet cells with IFN-γ increased MHC class I expression and increased lysis by the CTL clones.

Reference - Title: T cell receptor recognition of a 'super-bulged' major histocompatibility complex class I-bound peptide.
1st in vivo Process - Process Type: Environmental exposure to endemic/ubiquitous agent without evidence for disease
1st immunogen - Name: Human herpesvirus 4 strain B95-8 (Epstein-Barr virus (strain B95-8))
Immunization - Comments: Generation of the T Cell clone SB27 was previously described in the reference cited: Tynan et al. (2005) J Biol Chem 280: 23900-23909 [PMID: 15849183]. The SB27 TCR was expressed and purified.
Assay - Location of Assay Data in Refere: Tables 1, 2, Supplementary Table 1, Figures 1, 2, 5 and PDB 2AK4
Assay - Comments: There are four molecules in the crystallographic asymmetric unit. PDB chains for each complex are: Complex I: MHC α-chain: A, β2-m chain: B, epitope chain: C, TCR α-chain: D, TCR β-chain: E. Complex II: MHC α-chain: F, β2-m chain: G, epitope chain: H, TCR α-chain: I, TCR β-chain: J. Complex III: MHC α-chain: K, β2-m chain: L, epitope chain: M, TCR α-chain: N, TCR β-chain: P. Complex IV: MHC α-chain: Q, β2-m chain: R, epitope chain: S, TCR α-chain: T, TCR β-chain: U. All TCR-MHC/epitope complexes had well ordered electron density, and the electron density at the TCR-MHC/epitope interface was unambiguous. The individual TCR and MHC/epitope components were almost identical in all complexes. But, there was a TCR-MHC/epitope dimer present in the crystal lattice, made by complexes A (complex I) and B (complex IV). These complexes have distinct conformations, with the TCR adopting two different docking strategies on the MHC/epitope complex that differed by 12 degrees. This rotation axis was parallel to the peptide binding groove, causing atomic shifts in excess of 7 Å, resulting in leaning of the TCR more toward the MHC α2-helix. This assay refers to Complex A (complex I).

Immunization - Comments: Details about the production of the epitope-specific CD8+ T cells were not provided in the manuscript.
Assay - Comments: The epitope-specific T cell recognized antigen in a dose- and time- specific manner, and was quantified by IFN-g and GM-CSF. 1st in vivo Process - Process Type: Occurrence of infectious disease
Immunization - Comments: Samples were collected from one EBV-seronegative patient who underwent primary EBV infection following transplantation with grafts from EBV-seropositive donors.
Assay - Comments: NGS sequencing of TCR receptors in tetramer-sorted populations revealed that 1 or 2 clones dominated the response. Results were confirmed by FACS analysis. Among the total CD8+ cell population, the 1st, 4th, and 6th most abundant clones were directed against the epitope. The vast majority of the tetramer-positive clones identified during the early response had a very low precursor frequency. Analysis 3 years later revealed that the clonal repertoire does not change after the early phase, and virtually all clones are maintained at high frequencies. Similar results were observed in healthy patients exhibiting latent infection.

1st in vivo Process - Process Type: Exposure with existing immune reactivity without evidence for disease

Heatmap analysis shows that TRBV usage differed between young (18 to 22 years)  and older (> 60 years) donors in EBV-specific responses either when frequency was directly compared between the groups or if the hierarchy of TRBV usage within the group was examined. Significant differences were found in the number of glycines (Ai-v, number of nucleotide additions (Bi-v), and number of nucleotides per amino acids (Ci-v) between young and older adults and between the epitope specific and cross-reactive responses for TRAV and TRBV. Significant differences in TRAV and TRBV CDR3 lengths and family usage were observed between young and older donors.

1st in vivo Process - Process Type: Exposure with existing immune reactivity without evidence for disease
Immunization - Comments: Isolation of the TK3 TCR was described in the cited reference [PMID:17082594].  PBMCs from healthy, HLA-B*35:01+ EBV-sero positive volunteers were stimulated biweekly with the HPVG peptide to generate epitope specificT cell clones.  Isolated TCR α/ß genes were used to transduce a Jurkat reporter cell line.
Assay - Location of Assay Data in Refere: Figures 4 and S8 and Supplemental Dataset S1
Assay - Comments: Activation of Jurkat T cells expressing the epitope specific TCR by the HPVG analog was demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy.  Testing of a series of HPVG analogs showed the TK3 TCR had a strong preference for peptides with wildtype residues P2, G4, A6, D7, and in particular E10; but was also able to bind peptides with E5Q, Y8F, F9W, and Y11F substitutions.  The analogs were designed using HERMES, a 3D rotationally equivariant structure based neural network model, trained on the protein universe, which generated immunogenic peptides predicted to elicit strong TCR recognition when presented by MHC class I.

Reference - Title: De novo identification of the specificities of recurrently identified human T cell receptors.
1st in vivo Process - Process Type: Environmental exposure to endemic/ubiquitous agent without evidence for disease
Immunization - Comments: Isolation of epitope specific TCR #3 and TCR #5 was described in cited references [PMID: 23267020] and [PMID: 28369038], respectively.  TCR #3 was cloned and sequenced from tetramer sorted PBMC. TCR #5 was identified in public TCRß sequencing data representing TCRß sequences that were clonally expanded (defined as a frequency >0.001) in peripheral blood of >1 healthy donor. TCRß sequences that were recurrently found in donors typing for the same HLA allele were selected.
Assay - Comments: Jurkat T cells transduced with the epitope specific TCRs were activated by HeLa cells expressing the epitope and HLA-B*08:01 as demonstrated by AIMcap (activation-induced marker-mediated capture of target epitopes).  Jurkat cells were engineered to express a surface-anchored, high-affinity anti-IL-2 antibody, enabling live Jurkat cells to capture their own secreted IL-2.  Activation upon epitope stimulation was then assessed by accumulation of cell surface IL2 and CD69 upregulation.
